blocks.p: When Diabolus saw himself so boldly confronted by the Lord Mayor, and saw how stout-hearted Mr. Godly-Fear was, he flew into a rage and at once called a council of war, so that he might be revenged on Mansoul. So all the princes of the pit came together, with old Incredulity at the head of them and all the captains of his army, and they consult what to do. The whole business of the council that day was how they might take the castle; for they could not count themselves masters of the town so long as the castle was in the hands of their enemies.
So one advised this way and another that; but when they could not agree on a verdict, Apollyon, the president of the council, stood up and began.

“My brotherhood,” he said, “I have two things to propose to you, and my first is this. Let us withdraw from the town into the plain again. Our presence here will do us no good, because the castle is still in our enemies’ hands; nor is it possible for us to take it so long as so many brave captains are in it, and this bold fellow Godly-Fear is made keeper of its gates. Now, when we have withdrawn into the plain, they will be glad of a little ease, and it may be that, of their own accord, they will begin to grow careless again; and their carelessness will deal them a bigger blow than we could ever deal them ourselves. But if that should fail, our leaving the town may draw the captains out after us, and you know what it cost them when we fought them in the field before. Besides, if we can only draw them out into the field, we may lay an ambush behind the town, which, once they have come out, shall rush in and take possession of the castle.”

But Beelzebub stood up and replied, “It is impossible to draw them all away from the castle. Some, you may be sure, will stay there to keep it; so it would be useless to try this unless we were sure they would all come out.” He therefore concluded that what was to be done must be done by some other means. And the likeliest means that the greatest heads among them could invent was the one Apollyon had advised before: namely, to get the townsmen to sin again.

“For,” he said, “it is not our being in the town, or in the field, or our fighting, or our killing their men, that can make us masters of Mansoul. So long as one man in the town can lift a finger against us, Emmanuel will take their part; and if he takes their part, we know what time of day it will be with us. So in my judgment there is no way to bring them into bondage to us like inventing a way to make them sin. If we had left all our doubters at home, we would have done as well as we have done now, unless we could have made them masters and governors of the castle; for doubters kept at a distance are like objections already answered by argument. Indeed, if we can only get them into the stronghold and make them its owners, the day will be ours. Let us therefore withdraw into the plain (not expecting the captains in Mansoul to follow us); but, I say, before we do, let us confer again with our trusty Diabolonians who are still hiding in their holes in Mansoul, and set them to work to betray the town to us. For they are the ones who must do it, or it will be left undone forever.”

By these words of Beelzebub (for I think it was he who gave this counsel), the whole assembly was compelled to agree with him: that the way to get the castle was to get the town to sin. Then they began to devise by what means they might bring this about.

Then Lucifer stood up and said, “The counsel of Beelzebub is to the point. Now the way to bring it about, in my opinion, is this. Let us withdraw our forces from the town of Mansoul; and let us terrify them no more, either with summons, or threats, or the noise of our drum, or any other means that might wake them up. Let us only lie in the field at a distance, as if we took no notice of them; for frights, I see, only wake them and make them stand all the more to their arms.

“I have another stratagem in my head as well. You know Mansoul is a market town that delights in trade. What, then, if some of our Diabolonians pretend to be men from a far country, and bring some of our wares to sell in the market of Mansoul? And what does it matter at what price they sell them, even at half what they are worth? Only let those who trade there be clever men, and true to us, and I will stake my crown that it will work. Two have come to my mind already who will be masters at this work: Mr. Penny-wise-pound-foolish and Mr. Win-small-lose-big; and this man with the long name is not a bit behind the other. What if you join to them Mr. Sweet-world and Mr. Present-good? They are civil, cunning men, but our true friends and helpers. Let these, and as many more, take up this business for us; let Mansoul be taken up with much business, and let them grow full and rich; this is the way to gain ground on them. Do you not remember that this is how we prevailed over Laodicea, and how many we hold in this snare right now? Now when they begin to grow full, they will forget their misery; and if we do not frighten them, they may well fall asleep, and so be brought to neglect their town watch, their castle watch, and their watch at the gates as well.

“Yes, and by this means may we not so burden Mansoul with abundance that they will be forced to make their castle a warehouse, instead of a garrison fortified against us and a barracks for men of war? If we can get our goods and commodities in there, I reckon the castle is more than half ours. Besides, if we could arrange for it to be filled with wares of that kind, then if we made a sudden assault on them, it would be hard for the captains to take shelter there. Do you not know the saying in the parable, ‘The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word’? [Matt. 13:22] And again, that when ‘the heart is weighed down with self-indulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this life,’ every kind of mischief comes upon them unawares? [Luke 21:34]

“Furthermore, my lords,” he said, “you know very well that a people cannot be filled with our things without having some of our Diabolonians as hangers-on in their houses and service. Where is the Mansoulian full of this world who does not have for his servants and attendants Mr. Profuse, or Mr. Prodigality, or some other of our Diabolonian gang, such as Mr. Voluptuous, Mr. Busybody, Mr. Ostentation, or the like? Now these can take the castle of Mansoul, or blow it up, or make it unfit to garrison Emmanuel’s men; any one of them will do. Yes, for all I know, these may do it for us sooner than an army of twenty thousand men. So, to end where I began, my advice is that we quietly withdraw, offering no further force or forcible attempt upon the castle, at least for now; and let us set our new project on foot, and see whether it will not make them destroy themselves.”
This advice was highly applauded by them all, and was counted the very masterpiece of hell: to choke Mansoul with the fullness of this world, and to glut her heart with its good things.

But see how things come together! Just as this Diabolonian council broke up, Captain Credence received a letter from Emmanuel, and its contents were these: that on the third day he would meet him in the field, in the plains around Mansoul.
“Meet me in the field!” said the Captain. “What does my lord mean by this? I don’t know what he means by meeting me in the field.”

So he carried the note to my Lord Secretary to ask his opinion of it; for my Lord was a seer in all matters concerning the King, and also for the good and comfort of the town of Mansoul. “For my part,” said Captain Credence, “I don’t know what it means.”

So my Lord took it and read it, and after a little pause he said, “The Diabolonians have held a great consultation against Mansoul today. This very day, I say, they have been plotting the utter ruin of the town; and the result of their council is to set Mansoul on a course that, if she takes it, will surely make her destroy herself. To this end they are making ready to leave the town and take to the field again, and there to lie until they see whether this project of theirs will take or not. But be ready with your Lord’s men (for on the third day they will be in the plain) to fall on the Diabolonians there; for by that time the Prince will be in the field, yes, by break of day, at sunrise or before, and with a mighty force against them. So he will be in front of them, and you behind them, and between you both their army will be destroyed.”

When Captain Credence heard this, away he went to the rest of the captains and told them of the note he had received from Emmanuel. “And what was dark in it,” he said, “my lord the Lord Secretary has explained to me.” He told them, too, what he and they must do to answer their Lord’s mind. Then the captains were glad; and Captain Credence ordered all the King’s trumpeters to go up onto the battlements of the castle, and there, in the hearing of Diabolus and of the whole town of Mansoul, to make the best music that heart could invent.

The trumpeters did as they were commanded. They got themselves up to the top of the castle and began to sound. Then Diabolus started, and said, “What can this mean? They are not sounding Boot-and-saddle, or Horse-and-away, or a charge. What do these madmen mean, that they should still be so merry and glad?”
Then one of his own men answered, “This is for joy that their Prince Emmanuel is coming to relieve the town of Mansoul. He is at the head of an army for that purpose, and the relief is near.”
The men of Mansoul too were greatly stirred by this melodious charm of the trumpets. They said, yes, they answered one another, “This can be no harm to us; surely this can be no harm to us.”

Then the Diabolonians said, “What had we best do?” And the answer came that it was best to leave the town. “And that,” said one, “you may do in keeping with your last council; and by doing so you will also be better able to give the enemy battle, if an army should come on us from outside.”

So on the second day they withdrew from Mansoul into the plains outside, and encamped before Eye-gate in as earthly and terrible an array as they could. The reason they would not stay in the town (besides those debated in their late conclave) was that they did not hold the stronghold. “Besides,” they said, “we will have more room to fight, and to run if need be, encamped in the open plains.” What is more, the town would have been a pit for them rather than a place of defense, had the Prince come up and shut them in there. So they took to the field, to be out of reach of the slings as well, which had greatly troubled them all the while they were in the town.

Well, when the time came for the captains to fall on the Diabolonians, they eagerly prepared themselves for action; for Captain Credence had told the captains the night before that they would meet their Prince in the field the next day. This made them far more eager still to engage the enemy; for “You shall see the Prince in the field tomorrow” was like oil on a flaming fire, since they had long been at a distance from him.

So, as I said, when the hour came, Captain Credence and the rest of the men of war drew out their forces before daylight by the sally-port, the town’s small gate for sorties. And when all were ready, Captain Credence went up to the head of the army and gave the rest of the captains the word, and they gave it to their under-officers and soldiers. The word was “The sword of the Prince Emmanuel, and the shield of Captain Credence,” which in the Mansoulian tongue is “The word of God and faith.” Then the captains fell on, and began roundly to attack Diabolus’s camp in front, on the flank, and in the rear.

Now they had left Captain Experience in the town, because he was still ill from the wounds the Diabolonians had given him in the last fight. But when he saw that the captains were at it, what does he do but call for his crutches in haste, get up, and away to the battle, saying, “Shall I lie here when my brothers are in the fight, and when Emmanuel the Prince will show himself in the field to his servants?” And when the enemy saw the man coming on his crutches, they were all the more daunted. “For,” they thought, “what spirit has got into these Mansoulians, that they fight us on their crutches?”

Well, as I said, the captains fell on and handled their weapons bravely, crying out and shouting all the while as they laid on blows, “The sword of the Prince Emmanuel, and the shield of Captain Credence!”

Now when Diabolus saw that the captains had come out, and had surrounded his men so valiantly, he concluded that for the present nothing was to be expected from them but blows, and the cuts of their “two-edged sword.”

So he too fell on the Prince’s army with all his deadly force, and the battle was joined. And whom did Diabolus meet first in the fight but Captain Credence on one hand and the Lord Willbewill on the other! Now Willbewill’s blows were like the blows of a giant, for that man had a strong arm; and he fell on the Election-doubters, for they were Diabolus’s lifeguard, and he kept them busy a good while, cutting and battering them hard. When Captain Credence saw my lord engaged, he fell stoutly on the same company from the other side, and so they threw them into great disorder. Now Captain Good-Hope had engaged the Calling-doubters, and they were sturdy men; but the captain was a valiant man, and Captain Experience sent him some help as well; so he made the Calling-doubters retreat. The rest of the armies were hotly engaged on every side, and the Diabolonians fought stoutly. Then my Lord Secretary ordered the slings in the castle to be played, and his men could throw stones to a hair’s breadth.

But after a while, those who had been made to flee before the Prince’s captains began to rally, and came up stoutly on the rear of the Prince’s army; and the Prince’s army began to flag. But remembering that they would soon see the face of their Prince, they took courage, and a very fierce battle was fought. Then the captains shouted, “The sword of the Prince Emmanuel, and the shield of Captain Credence!” and at that Diabolus fell back, thinking that more help had come. But still no Emmanuel appeared. The battle hung in doubt, and both sides drew back a little. Now in this breathing space Captain Credence bravely encouraged his men to stand firm, and Diabolus did the same as well as he could. But Captain Credence made a brave speech to his soldiers, and this is what he said:

“Gentlemen soldiers, my brothers in this enterprise, it gladdens me greatly to see in the field for our Prince today so stout and valiant an army, and such faithful lovers of Mansoul. Up to now, as becomes you, you have shown yourselves men of truth and courage against the Diabolonian forces, so that for all their boasting they have little yet to boast of in what they have gained. Now take up your old courage, and show yourselves men just this once more; for within a few minutes of the next engagement, this time, you will see your Prince show himself in the field. We must make this second assault on this tyrant Diabolus, and then Emmanuel comes.”

No sooner had the captain made this speech to his soldiers than one Mr. Speedy came riding hard to the captain from the Prince, to tell him that Emmanuel was at hand. When the captain received this news, he passed it on to the other field officers, and they to their soldiers and men of war. Then, like men raised from the dead, the captains and their men rose up, made for the enemy, and cried as before, “The sword of the Prince Emmanuel, and the shield of Captain Credence!”

The Diabolonians bestirred themselves too, and resisted as well as they could; but in this last engagement they lost their courage, and many of the doubters fell dead to the ground. Now when they had been in the heat of battle about an hour or more, Captain Credence lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, Emmanuel came! He came with colors flying and trumpets sounding, and the feet of his men scarcely touched the ground, so fast did they hurry toward the captains who were engaged. Then Credence wheeled his men toward the town and left Diabolus the field; so Emmanuel came on him from one side, and the enemy lay between them both. Then they fell to it again afresh; and now it was only a little while before Emmanuel and Captain Credence met, trampling down the slain as they came.

But when the captains saw that the Prince had come, and that he had fallen on the Diabolonians from the other side, and that Captain Credence and his Highness had them penned between them, they shouted (they shouted so that the ground split again), “The sword of Emmanuel, and the shield of Captain Credence!” Now when Diabolus saw that he and his forces were so hard pressed by the Prince and his princely army, what did he and the lords of the pit who were with him do but make their escape, desert their army, and leave them to fall by the hand of Emmanuel and of his noble Captain Credence. So they all fell down slain before them, before the Prince and before his royal army. Not so much as one doubter was left alive; they lay spread on the ground, dead men, as one would spread dung on the land.
